results.claim: Planar two-exit instances admit a cyclic two-gate decomposition. Let the exits be p,q and let B=N(p)∩N(q). Every component of G−({p,q}∪B) is adjacent to at most two vertices of B; when |B|≥3, those two are consecutive in the cyclic order of B around the exits.
results.proof_sketch: The edges from {p,q} to B form K_{2,|B|}. For |B|≥3, every face of a planar embedding of this subgraph is a 4-cycle p-b_i-q-b_{i+1}-p: Euler's formula gives |B| faces, and bipartiteness makes every face length at least four, forcing equality throughout. A connected subgraph disjoint from K_{2,|B|} lies in one of these faces, so it can meet only the two B-vertices on that face boundary. For |B|≤2 the assertion is immediate. Thus all non-skeleton complexity occurs in planar pieces with at most two common-neighbor gates.

results.claim: There is a linear-time classification when the exits have the same independent neighborhood. After deleting a possible irrelevant edge pq, suppose N(p)=N(q)=B and B is independent. The fugitive wins exactly when (i) s∈{p,q}∪B, (ii) s has a neighbor in B, or (iii) s has a neighbor w having two distinct neighbors in B.
results.proof_sketch:
The three conditions give explicit wins. In (ii), move directly to an untouched b∈B; after Nemesis deletes one of bp,bq, use the other. In (iii), move to w. The three-edge sets {wb_i,b_ip,b_iq} for two gates b_1,b_2 are edge-disjoint, so one deletion spoils at most one; move to the other gate and escape.

Conversely, assume none holds. Call b prepared if one of bp,bq is deleted and dead if both are deleted. After the fugitive's first move to w, let C be its component outside {p,q}∪B. By the preceding decomposition, C has at most two boundary gates. Since w is adjacent to at most one of them, Nemesis prepares that one, or an arbitrary boundary gate if w sees none. Before the other gate can be entered, Nemesis gets another deletion with which to prepare it. Whenever a prepared gate is entered, she immediately deletes its other exit edge, making it dead. From a dead gate, the fugitive cannot move directly to another gate because B is independent. If he enters another outside component, that component contains the dead gate among its at most two boundary gates, so there is at most one new gate; Nemesis prepares it after the first move into the component. Induction prevents entry into any unprepared gate. Since an edge is deleted every round, play terminates without escape. The stated conditions are testable by adjacency scans.

results.claim: Two broader target-relevant subclasses are linearly solvable: (a) the graph induced by regular vertices is a forest, with arbitrary degrees; or (b) every regular vertex has degree at most three, with arbitrary exit degrees.
results.proof_sketch: Replace every incidence vx of an exit x by an edge from v to a fresh degree-one exit x_v, and remove the original exits. This preserves the game exactly: entering an exit ends play, so exits are never useful as transit vertices, and deletions of exit incidences correspond one-for-one. In case (a), the transformed starting component is a tree. In case (b), the transformed graph has maximum degree at most three because only exits were split. The source paper's proved linear-time theorem for trees and maximum-degree-three graphs therefore applies. This also strengthens its degree restriction: high degrees at the two exits themselves cause no difficulty.

results.claim: The binary-escape-tree condition is not necessary even for planar simple graphs with exactly two exits. A seven-vertex counterexample has exits p,q, start s, regular vertices a,b,c,z, and edges pa,pb,qa,qb,ab,az,bz,bc,cz,cs.
results.proof_sketch:
The graph is planar: draw the four internally disjoint a-b paths ab, a-p-b, a-q-b, and a-z-b as nested arcs; draw b-c-z in a face incident with bz and attach the leaf s at c.

The fugitive moves s→c. If Nemesis deletes bc, move c→z. Her next deletion can spoil at most one of the two edge-disjoint escape configurations z-a-{p,q} and z-b-{p,q}; move through the other common neighbor and then take the surviving exit edge. If the first deletion is not bc, move c→b. At the next fugitive turn, use bp or bq if either remains. If both have been deleted, those are exactly Nemesis's first two deletions, so ab,ap,aq remain; move b→a and then use whichever of ap,aq survives.

Nevertheless the tree condition fails after splitting exit incidences into degree-one exit copies. The only possible roots within distance one of s are s and c. Vertex s has only one edge. A full binary tree rooted at c cannot use regular leaf s, so its children must be b,z. Since z has no exit neighbor, its two children would have to be a,b, repeating b from the other root branch. Hence no such tree exists.

results.claim: An exact recurrence gives PSPACE membership and an O*(8^n) planar algorithm, although not a polynomial classification. For deleted-edge set D and current regular vertex v, W(D,v) holds iff some surviving move vw reaches an exit or, for every surviving edge e Nemesis might delete, w remains connected to an exit and W(D∪{e},w) holds.
results.proof_sketch: Each recursive call adds one deleted edge, so the recurrence is acyclic and exactly matches the move order and quantifiers. There are at most n·2^m states and only polynomial work per move/deletion pair, giving O*(2^m) time with memoization. A planar simple graph has m≤3n−6, hence O*(8^n). Depth-first evaluation stores only a polynomial-depth path and polynomial-size states, proving PSPACE membership.

final_writeup:
This is a partial resolution. I did not obtain either a polynomial-time algorithm for all planar simple two-exit instances or a complete hardness reduction.

The main structural leverage is that the common neighbors of the two exits form a planar K_{2,k} skeleton. Its faces arrange those gates cyclically, and every remaining connected piece can touch at most two consecutive gates. Using this, the game is completely classified in linear time when both exits have the same neighborhood and that neighborhood is independent: the only winning configurations are an immediate gate, a gate one move away, or a first move exposing two gates simultaneously. Nemesis otherwise prepares and then kills boundary gates while following the fugitive from face to face.

Exit splitting also yields two substantial linear-time cases: arbitrary-degree instances whose regular core is a forest, and instances in which only the exits may have degree above three.

The seven-vertex construction shows why these results do not immediately extend to all planar two-exit graphs. A single edge between common-neighbor gates, combined with a small planar backup cycle, lets the fugitive win from distance two from every binary escape-tree root even though the paper's tree condition fails. Thus a general algorithm must account for tempo gained by moving through partially damaged gates; static escape-tree detection alone cannot classify the target.

The remaining unresolved core consists of the cyclic gate skeleton with edges or more general short connections between consecutive gates and arbitrary planar two-boundary pieces between them. The exact recurrence supplies a rigorous exponential baseline and PSPACE upper bound, but no matching lower bound is established here.
checks_performed: Read only the designated JSON input; used no web sources and no other repository files.
Implemented the stated exact recurrence using integer edge masks. On the seven-vertex counterexample it returned a fugitive win after evaluating 164 distinct game states.
After splitting the four exit incidences in the counterexample, exhaustively inspected all 1,023 nonempty edge subsets separately for roots s and c; none formed a rooted full binary escape tree.

Exhaustively checked the independent-neighborhood classification on 2,514 labeled finite graphs satisfying the two-gate attachment property, with one to three gates and at most three other regular vertices, for every possible start. No discrepancy with the criterion was found. This check supplements, but is not used in place of, the proof.
